stem: Which organism is most likely?
case_text: A 55-year-old has a foul-smelling, gas-forming abscess after colon surgery. Culture grows a gram-negative anaerobic rod that is bile-resistant, blackens on blood agar, and grows rapidly; it is resistant to penicillin.
explanation: Bacteroides fragilis is a bile-resistant, penicillin-resistant anaerobic, gram-negative rod commonly isolated after lower-GI surgery. E. coli and Pseudomonas are aerobes; C. perfringens is a gram-positive rod associated with gas gangrene.

stem: Which test confirms the cause?
case_text: A child with a sore throat and fever has pharyngeal culture showing small, beta-hemolytic colonies; the bacitracin disk shows a zone of inhibition, and the group A streptococcal antigen test is positive.
explanation: Beta-hemolytic colony with bacitracin sensitivity and a positive Group A antigen test identifies S. pyogenes (group A strep), implicated in pharyngitis and post-streptococcal rheumatic fever.

stem: Which risk factor is most associated with this organism?
case_text: A pregnant woman who ate unpasteurized soft cheese develops fever, meningitis and stillbirth. CSF shows small gram-positive rods and grows an organism with tumbling motility at 25 C but not 37 C.
explanation: Listeria monocytogenes causes foodborne infection (unpasteurized dairy), meningitis in immunocompromised/pregnant patients and is a gram-positive rod with tumbling motility. Group B strep is a coccus; C. diphtheriae is associated with pseudomembranes.

stem: Which test is the most useful?
case_text: A 60-year-old smoker with pneumonia acquired from a contaminated hotel water system. Gram stain shows small gram-negative coccobacilli; culture on buffered charcoal yeast extract is positive; routine blood agar does not grow it; Legionella urinary antigen is positive.
explanation: L. pneumophila is a fastidious gram-negative coccobacillus that grows on buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) and is detected by urinary antigen. It is associated with water aerosols and does not grow on standard agar.

stem: Which organism is the likely cause?
case_text: A healthy 22-year-old presents with a painful, drained skin abscess after playing contact sports; it is not healed on first-line beta-lactam antibiotics. Culture shows S. aureus that is resistant to oxacillin/cefoxitin but susceptible to clindamycin.
explanation: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) causes skin/soft tissue infections in otherwise healthy people and is resistant to oxacillin/cefoxitin (mecA positive) but often susceptible to clindamycin/trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

stem: Which test best confirms the diagnosis?
case_text: A 20-year-old with paroxysmal cough and inspiratory whoop for 3 weeks. A nasopharyngeal swab is sent; the organism is small, gram-negative coccobacillus and grows only on Bordet-Gengou/Regan-Lowe medium; PCR is positive.
explanation: B. pertussis causes whooping cough and is a small gram-negative coccobacillus that requires Bordet-Gengou/Regan-Lowe medium; PCR is the most sensitive test, especially late in the illness.

stem: Which finding is most characteristic?
case_text: An HIV-positive patient with a low CD4 count and progressive dyspnea has a bronchoalveolar lavage. Silver (methenamine) stain shows thin-walled cysts and an organism that does not grow on routine fungal media.
explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly P. carinii) causes pneumonia in immunocompromised hosts, stains with silver (cyst walls), and cannot be cultured routinely. The classic morphologic finding is a foamy alveolar exudate.

stem: Which organism is identified?
case_text: An immunocompromised patient with a lung abscess has a moderately acid-fast, beaded, branching filamentous organism growing on agar; it is positive with a modified Kinyoun stain.
explanation: Nocardia is a weakly acid-fast, filamentous, branching bacterium (aerobic actinomycete) that causes pulmonary infection in immunocompromised patients; it is detected with a modified acid-fast stain. M. tuberculosis is strongly acid-fast but not filamentous.

stem: Which HIV management threshold is being applied?
case_text: An HIV-positive patient's CD4 count is 120 cells/uL. Which prophylactic measure is indicated?
explanation: Pneumocystis (and toxoplasma) prophylaxis is recommended when CD4 <200 cells/uL (especially <200; toxoplasma when <100). Antiretroviral therapy is indicated for all HIV patients regardless of CD4 count.

stem: Which mechanism underlies this reaction?
case_text: One week after receiving an antiserum (e.g., anti-thymocyte globulin or a large protein), a patient develops fever, urticaria, arthralgia, and low complement with circulating immune complexes.
explanation: Serum sickness is a type III hypersensitivity reaction mediated by immune complexes that deposit in tissues, causing vasculitis, fever, arthralgia and low complement. Type I is immediate (IgE); type II involves cell-surface antibodies.

stem: Which test finding best supports the diagnosis?
case_text: A 25-year-old with hemoptysis and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Lung/kidney biopsy shows linear immunoglobulin (and C3) deposition along the glomerular basement membrane, and the serum is positive.
explanation: Linear IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane with pulmonary hemorrhage is diagnostic of anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease. SLE shows granular deposits; ANCA-associated disease (GPA) is pauci-immune.

stem: Which antibody is most specific for this disorder?
case_text: A 40-year-old with symmetric, small joint pain and morning stiffness. Which antibody has the highest specificity for rheumatoid arthritis?
explanation: Anti-CCP is highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid factor is sensitive but less specific (found in many conditions). Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are specific for SLE.

stem: Which diagnosis is most consistent?
case_text: An infant with recurrent infections, congenital heart defect and low T-cell numbers has a small thymus and hypocalcemia; deletion on chromosome 22q11 is present.
explanation: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) is characterized by thymic hypoplasia causing T-cell deficiency, cardiac defects and hypocalcemia from parathyroid hypoplasia. SCID has both B and T cell defects without cardiac/hypocalcemia.

stem: Which test distinguishes active from treated infection?
case_text: A patient with suspected syphilis has a positive nontreponemal RPR (1:16) that remains positive after adequate treatment, while the treponemal FTA-ABS is also positive.
options: RPR titre confirms active infection; FTA-ABS confirms past/current treponemal exposure
FTA-ABS is screening; RPR is confirmatory
explanation: Nontreponemal tests (RPR/VDRL) are quantitative and used for screening/monitoring; a falling titre indicates response. Treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, TPPA) confirm treponemal exposure. A treated patient may have a persistently positive FTA-ABS.

stem: Which location of disease is indicated?
case_text: A 30-year-old with hypertension, hematuria and edema. Urine microscopy shows red cell casts.
explanation: Red cell casts localize bleeding and inflammation to the glomerulus, indicating glomerulonephritis. They are not seen in lower UTI, stones, or bladder tumors.

stem: Which finding best localizes the source?
case_text: A patient with hematuria. The urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells (acanthocytes), but phase-contrast microscopy shows mostly such cells.
explanation: Dysmorphic red cells and acanthocytes (spur cells) indicate glomerular bleeding. Normal (isomorphic) red cells suggest a lower urinary tract source.

stem: Which CSF pattern is most consistent?
case_text: A 28-year-old with subacute headache and low-grade fever, immigrant from a high-TB area. CSF: WBC 220 (85% lymphocytes), protein 140 mg/dL, glucose 25 mg/dL (serum glucose 90).
explanation: Lymphocytic pleocytosis with low glucose (low CSF:serum ratio), high protein, and a subacute course are classic for tuberculous or fungal meningitis. Viral meningitis has normal glucose; bacterial has polymorphonuclear cells.

stem: Which mechanism best explains these results?
case_text: A cirrhotic patient has massive ascites. The serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) is 1.4 g/dL.
explanation: A SAAG >1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension (transudative ascites). SAAG <1.1 suggests an exudative cause such as malignancy, infection (tuberculosis) or pancreatic disease.

stem: Which diagnosis is most consistent?
case_text: A 45-year-old with a swollen, hot, very painful knee. Synovial fluid: WBC 60,000/uL with 90% neutrophils and the analysis is culture-positive for gram-positive cocci in clusters.
explanation: A markedly inflamed joint with >50,000 WBC/uL (neutrophilic) and a positive culture indicates septic arthritis, most often due to S. aureus. Gout/pseudogout show crystals and are typically culture-negative.

stem: Which crystals are most likely?
case_text: A 50-year-old with acute, painful podagra (first metatarsophalangeal joint). Synovial fluid shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals.
explanation: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals are classic for monosodium urate (gout). Calcium pyrophosphate crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent (pseudogout).
